result.markdown: --- title: "Integrals" engine: julia --- A negative `derivative` order gives an interpolant of an integral: `derivative = -1` is the antiderivative, `-2` the twofold integral, and so on. Like the derivatives, integrals are evaluated analytically from the kernel's polynomial pieces, not by quadrature, and they are anchored at the first knot: there the integral is zero, and so are all lower integrals. So the antiderivative evaluated at $b$ is $\int_{x_0}^{b}$ of the interpolant, and a definite integral between two limits is the difference of two evaluations. ## A first example ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Julia ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} x = range(0, 2π, length = 40) # 40 uniformly spaced samples y = sin.(x) # the values at the samples i1 = convolution_interpolation(x, y; derivative = -1) # the integral from x[1] = 0 i2 = convolution_interpolation(x, y; derivative = -2) # the twofold integral, also anchored at 0 a, b = 1.0, 2.5 # the limits of a definite integral i1(1.0), i2(1.0), i1(b) - i1(a) # 1 − cos(1), 1 − sin(1), cos(a) − cos(b) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (0.45969769434630703, 0.15852901543032516, 1.3414459211930763) ``` ::: ::: ## Python ```python import numpy as np from convinterp import convolution_interpolation x = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 40) # 40 uniformly spaced samples y = np.sin(x) # the values at the samples i1 = convolution_interpolation(x, y, derivative=-1) # the integral from x[0] = 0 i2 = convolution_interpolation(x, y, derivative=-2) # the twofold integral, also anchored at 0 a, b = 1.0, 2.5 # the limits of a definite integral i1(1.0), i2(1.0), i1(b) - i1(a) # 1 − cos(1), 1 − sin(1), cos(a) − cos(b) ``` ::: | | ∫₀¹ f | ∫₀¹∫₀ˢ f | ∫ₐᵇ f | |:--|--:|--:|--:| | interpolant | 0.459697694346 | 0.158529015430 | 1.341445921193 | | exact | 0.459697694132 | 0.158529015192 | 1.341445921415 | ## Integrals don't cost convergence order Where each derivative order costs one order of convergence, integrals cost none: the integral of the interpolant converges at least as fast as the interpolant itself. Runge's function with `:b7`, the interpolant and its first and second integrals: ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The convergence study"} runge(x) = 1 / (1 + 25x^2) # Runge's function irunge = (x -> (atan(5x) + atan(5)) / 5, # its integral from −1 x -> (x * (atan(5x) + atan(5)) - log(1 + 25x^2) / 10 + log(26) / 10) / 5) # its twofold integral from −1 xr = range(-1, 1, length = 2001) # fine points for measuring the error ns = [41, 81, 161, 321, 641, 1281] # the numbers of samples hs = 2 ./ (ns .- 1) # the corresponding spacings orders = 0:-1:-2 # the interpolant and two integrals exact = (runge, irunge...) # the function and its integrals errors = [begin xn = range(-1, 1, length = n) itp_m = convolution_interpolation(xn, runge.(xn); kernel = :b7, derivative = m) maximum(abs.(itp_m.(xr) .- exact[1-m].(xr))) end for n in ns, m in orders] fig = Figure(size = (800, 420)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xreversed = true, xlabel = "spacing h", ylabel = "largest error") for (j, m) in enumerate(orders) scatterlines!(ax, hs, max.(errors[:, j], 1e-17); markersize = 8, label = m == 0 ? "interpolant" : "integral order $(-m)") end Legend(fig[1, 2], ax) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: | | interpolant | integral order 1 | integral order 2 | |:--|--:|--:|--:| | observed convergence order | 7.12 | 8.00 | 7.82 | Evaluating an integral costs about the same as evaluating the interpolant, whatever the number of knots: the contribution of every knot left of the stencil is a polynomial in the position within the cell, and those are precomputed when the interpolant is built. Each kernel supports integrals up to a fixed order, 2 for `:a0` and `:a1`, 4 for the other `:a` kernels, 6 for `:b5` and 8 for `:b7` to `:b13`; the precomputed tables grow with the order, so high orders in several dimensions cost memory. ## Integrals in more dimensions In more dimensions the orders are given per axis, and integrals combine freely with interpolation and derivatives along the other axes. The antiderivative along every axis is the iterated integral from the corner of the grid; a derivative along one axis and an integral along another is a Leibniz-rule operator, in one evaluation: ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Julia ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} xg = range(0, 2π, length = 60) # knots along x yg = range(0, 2π, length = 60) # knots along y data = [sin(xi) * cos(yi) for xi in xg, yi in yg] # sin(x)·cos(y) on the grid ixy = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; derivative = (-1, -1)) # ∫∫ from (0, 0) ix = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; derivative = (-1, 0)) # ∫ dx, interpolated in y dxiy = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; derivative = (1, -1)) # ∂/∂x ∫ dy ixy(1.0, 2.0), ix(1.0, 2.0), dxiy(1.0, 2.0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (0.4180019303973203, -0.19130174119961763, 0.49129549731347355) ``` ::: ::: ## Python ```python xg = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 60) # knots along x yg = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 60) # knots along y data = np.sin(xg)[:, None] * np.cos(yg)[None, :] # sin(x)·cos(y) on the grid ixy = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data, derivative=(-1, -1)) # ∫∫ from (0, 0) ix = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data, derivative=(-1, 0)) # ∫ dx, interpolated in y dxiy = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data, derivative=(1, -1)) # ∂/∂x ∫ dy ixy(1.0, 2.0), ix(1.0, 2.0), dxiy(1.0, 2.0) ``` ::: | at (1, 2) | ∫₀¹∫₀² f | ∫₀¹ f dx | ∂/∂x ∫₀² f dy | |:--|--:|--:|--:| | interpolant | 0.418001930397 | -0.191301741200 | 0.491295497313 | | exact | 0.418001930392 | -0.191301741181 | 0.491295496434 | ## Discontinuous data The `:a0` kernel, which is nearest-neighbour interpolation, integrates piecewise-constant data exactly: a spike one cell wide and $1/h$ high integrates to a unit step, which is how a sampled impulse should behave. ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} n = 1001 # knots xs = range(0, 2π, length = n) h = step(xs) # the spacing spike = [abs(xi - π) < h / 2 ? 1 / h : 0.0 for xi in xs] # a unit-area spike at π F = convolution_interpolation(xs, spike; kernel = :a0, derivative = -1) # its integral xf = range(0, 2π, length = 801) fig = Figure(size = (800, 400)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "x") lines!(ax, xf, F.(xf); label = "∫ spike") lines!(ax, xf, (xf .> π) .* 1.0; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "unit step") Legend(fig[1, 2], ax) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Nonuniform grids Integrals are available on uniform grids only, in both packages; the nonuniform kernels of the Julia package support interpolation and derivatives but not antiderivatives. The [nonuniform page](nonuniform.qmd) says what to do instead.
